title: Inhibitor segregation can make a nonexplosive reaction network explode
shortTitle: When dividing compartments throw away the brakes
oneLine: Two simple chemistries that are safe on their own explode once dividing compartments keep the substrate together and export the inhibitor, with no inflow reactions or fusion; the exact thresholds are d + λE[log Q] < b and bλ(1 − EQ) > dc.
abstract: A stochastic chemical system explodes when infinitely many reaction events occur in finite time. Anderson, Howells and Rojas La Luz (2026) conjectured that a nonexplosive chemistry stays nonexplosive inside dividing compartments and pointed to inflow reactions as the main danger. This candidate gives two two-species chemistries with no inflow reaction, no compartment fusion and no exit that are nonexplosive alone but explode with positive probability once compartments divide at a rate proportional to their substrate, keep all substrate in one daughter and retain each inhibitor with a possibly random probability Q. For conversion inhibition (2S→3S, S→S+I, S+I→2I) explosion is possible exactly when d+λE[log Q]<b; for catalytic inhibition (I+2S→I+S) exactly when bλ(1−EQ)>dc; both boundaries are nonexplosive. The candidate proves exact conditional explosion laws, blow-up asymptotics, monotonicity and continuity at threshold, and robustness to bounded substrate leakage. Comparison with a well-mixed degradation reaction removing the same mean amount of inhibitor isolates the compartmental effect: a strictly larger explosive region for the self-reproducing inhibitor, the same threshold for the catalytic one. For a three-molecule example the explosion probability is at least 1/2 and lies in [0.79744, 0.79751]. The probabilistic components are classical and cited; Yoo (2026) reported an earlier counterexample to the unrestricted conjecture using inflow and fusion. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Conversion inhibition (Theorem 3.1, proof): with 2S→3S at bs(s−1), S→S+I at cs and S+I→2I at dsi, d>b, the chemistry is nonexplosive alone; with division at rate λs keeping all S together and each inhibitor kept with probability p, explosion has positive probability iff d+λ log p<b, and is impossible at equality.

Exact law (Theorem 3.1(f), proof): conditional on the inhibitor history, the explosion probability is the chance that fewer than s₀−1 independent coins with success probabilities e^(−bτⱼ) succeed, τⱼ being the conversion times; on explosion (T−t)S(t)→1/b (Theorem 3.3).
Catalytic inhibition (Theorem 4.1, proof): with I+2S→I+S at dis(s−1), explosion has positive probability iff bλ(1−p)>dc, and the conditional probability is 1−(1−1/(bD∞))^(s₀−1).
Random retention (Theorems 5.1–5.2, proof): thresholds d+λE[log Q]<b and bλ(1−EQ)>dc; two division rules with the same mean retention can put the conversion chemistry on opposite sides.

What compartments add (Theorem 6.1, Corollary 6.2, Proposition 6.3, proof): removing the same mean amount of inhibitor by a well-mixed reaction S+I→S gives the strictly smaller explosive region λ(1−EQ)>d−b for conversion and the same threshold for catalysis.

Monotonicity, continuity, leakage (Propositions 6.4–6.5, proof): the explosion probability falls as more inhibitor is kept, tends to zero at both thresholds, and stays positive if each division leaks a bounded number of substrate molecules.

Worked example (Theorem 3.2 and Section 7.1): for b=c=1, d=2, λ=3, all inhibitor exported, from (S,I)=(3,0), P(explosion)≥1/2, and a deterministic computation with rounding control gives P(explosion)∈[0.79744, 0.79751].

narration: When dividing compartments throw away the brakes. An Evidence Press briefing. Many reactions in living cells happen inside compartments that grow and divide. Mathematicians model this with random chemistry in every compartment, and a compartment that splits in two from time to time. A good model of this kind should never explode, meaning it should never pack infinitely many reactions into a finite stretch of time. A recent paper conjectured that if the chemistry is safe on its own, it stays safe inside dividing compartments, and it pointed to reactions that create molecules from nothing as the main danger. This release shows that removing those reactions is not enough. Picture a substance that makes more of itself, and an inhibitor that holds it in check. In one compartment the inhibitor wins and nothing goes wrong. Now let compartments divide so that all of the substance stays in one daughter, while the inhibitor may leave with the other. Each division throws away some of the brakes, and the substance can then run away. In a small example the paper proves that this happens with probability at least one half, and computes the probability as about eighty per cent. The paper finds the exact boundary between safety and runaway for two kinds of inhibitor. When the inhibitor multiplies, what matters is the average of the logarithm of the share it keeps at each division, so dividing in bulk is more dangerous than steady removal at the same average rate. When the inhibitor does not multiply, only the average share matters. On both boundaries the model stays safe. The building blocks are classical results about branching processes, which the paper cites; the new part is the chemical construction and its exact classification. An earlier preprint by Yoo had already found a different counterexample using other ingredients. The results have written proofs and computer checks. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on 31 October 2026, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: Two two-species chemistries with no inflow, fusion or exit that are nonexplosive alone but explode with positive probability under substrate-keeping, inhibitor-segregating division; sharp thresholds, exact conditional laws, comparison with well-mixed removal, continuity at threshold and an enclosed example probability.
decisionObject.scope: The compartment framework of Anderson, Howells and Rojas La Luz (2026) with no inflow, exit or coagulation, and kernels keeping all substrate in one daughter (bounded leakage allowed for the explosive direction). Molecule-blind kernels are not addressed.
